Field Overview

The V5RC Override Field consists of the following:

  • 56 Cups
    • 20 Match Loads
      • 10 for red Alliance

    • 24 that start the Match in predetermined locations on the Field (gray side up)
    • 12 that start the Match in predetermined locations on the Field (clear side up)
  • 63 Pins

    • 20 red/yellow

    • 20 blue/yellow
      • 2 Preloads
      • 10 Match Loads
      • 8 that start the Match in predetermined locations
    • 19 yellow/yellow
      • 2 Match Loads
      • 17 that start the Match in predetermined locations
  • 9 Goals
    • 4 Alliance colored
      • 2 red
      • 2 blue

docs.title: Identify
docs.text:
We need to understand Override well enough to decide the most effective way to score. The plan is to work out the absolute maximum score the game allows, then look at what that maximum is made of. Whatever makes up most of the ceiling is the most point-dense method available, so that's what we design around.

The game. Override (V5RC 2026-2027) is played on a 12' x 12' square field. Head-to-head matches are 2v2: a red alliance and a blue alliance, two teams each.

Match structure:

  • Autonomous Period: 0:15 (no drivers)
  • Driver Controlled Period: 1:45
  • Endgame: the last 0:10 of driver control, "king of the hill" in the midfield

The object: score more than the other alliance by (1) stacking Pins and Cups onto Goals, (2) setting Toggles to your color to own yellow pins in that quadrant, and (3) ending the match with your Robot in the contested Midfield.

Scoring:

Action Points Autonomous Bonus (1 alliance) 12 Each scored alliance-color pin half 5 Each scored yellow pin half (owned) 10 Each robot in the Midfield (end) 8

Plus the Autonomous Win Point (ranking WP, not match points) for completing the auton task set with no violations.

Field Objects:

Appendix - Field Overview

Field Overview

The V5RC Override Field consists of the following:

  • 56 Cups
    • 20 Match Loads
      • 10 for red Alliance
      • 10 for blue Alliance
    • 24 that start the Match in predetermined locations on the Field (gray side up)
    • 12 that start the Match in predetermined locations on the Field (clear side up)
  • 63 Pins
    • 4 red/blue that start the Match in predetermined locations
    • 20 red/yellow
      • 2 Preloads
      • 10 Match Loads
      • 8 that start the Match in predetermined locations
    • 20 blue/yellow
      • 2 Preloads
      • 10 Match Loads
      • 8 that start the Match in predetermined locations
    • 19 yellow/yellow
      • 2 Match Loads
      • 17 that start the Match in predetermined locations
  • 9 Goals
    • 4 Alliance colored
      • 2 red
      • 2 blue
    • 5 neutral colored
      • 4 short
      • 1 tall
  • 4 Toggles
  • 4 Loaders, two adjacent to each Alliance Station

A few things stand out about how this game works:

  • Toggles are a fast, cheap way to swing a lot of points, since flipping one lets you own all the yellow in a quadrant
  • Possession is capped at 1 pin + 1 cup, which caps how fast you can score more than it caps how much.
  • The last 10 seconds in the midfield decide both the 8pt/robot swing and who owns the midfield yellow.

docs.title: Max Score
docs.text:
What is the absolute ceiling?

Counting the pin halves. Each pin has 2 halves. 63 pins → 126 halves. The pin/cup/goal counts come from the Field Overview embedded above:

Pin type Count Red halves Blue halves Yellow halves red/blue 4 4 4 0 red/yellow 20 20 0 20 blue/yellow 20 0 20 20 yellow/yellow 19 0 0 38 total 63 24 24 78

Cups do the covering. A half only scores while it stays visible, and the thing that hides a half is a cup: each cup joins two stacked pins and covers exactly one of the two halves meeting it, whichever one sits in its opaque side. Rotate the cup and you pick which. That's what saves the red/blue pins: they have no yellow half, but you can still hide them completely by seating each between two cups with the opaque sides facing in, so both halves vanish and the neighbors show yellow instead. We have 56 cups against just 48 non-yellow halves (24 + 24), so nothing but yellow ever has to show.

So how many halves stay visible? Covering costs cups, and cups are also what let you stack. To place all 63 pins you build them onto the 7 goals you can reach (your 2 + 5 neutral; the opponent's 2 are off-limits). 63 pins in 7 stacks takes 63 − 7 = 56 cup joints, and each joint hides one half. So 56 halves get buried and 126 − 56 = 70 stay visible — all of them yellow (owning them needs all 4 toggle quadrants + the midfield):

Source Points 70 shown yellow halves (10 each) 700 2 robots in the midfield (8 each) 16 Autonomous bonus 12 Absolute max (1 alliance) 728

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
The number itself matters less than what it's made of:

  • 700 of the 728 points (96%) are yellow. Every non-yellow half gets buried under a cup, even both halves of the red/blue pins, so nothing but yellow shows. Yellow is really the whole scoring plan, and alliance-color halves are just the fallback when you can't get yellow up.
  • Yellow only counts when you own it, and ownership comes from toggles (per quadrant) and midfield majority (endgame). That makes a toggle flip the most point-dense action in the game: one flip turns a whole quadrant of yellow from 0 to 10 each, and zeroes out the opponent's yellow there at the same time. It swings both ways at once.
  • The real limit is cycle time, not stack height. SG6 caps possession at 1 pin + 1 cup, so every score is a round trip. What we're actually short on is owned-yellow placements per second.

Chosen scoring method (ranked by points-per-action):

  1. Flip toggles → own a quadrant of yellow (huge swing, one cheap action)
  2. Place yellow pins in quadrants/midfield you own (10/half)
  3. Hold the midfield at endgame (8/robot + owns midfield yellow + tiebreaker)
  4. Alliance-color pins (5/half) only when yellow/toggles aren't available

docs.title: Rule Analysis
docs.text: What is allowed?

docs.title: Subsystems:
docs.text:
Vex has 3 subsystems. What are they? and what limitations do they bring.

The rulebook states subsystem 1 and 2 as: "Subsystem 1: Mobile robotic base including wheels, tracks, legs, or any other mechanism that allows the Robot to navigate the majority of the flat playing Field surface. For a stationary Robot, the robotic base without wheels would be considered Subsystem 1. Subsystem 2: Power and control system that includes a legal VEX battery, a legal VEX control system, and associated motors for the mobile robotic base."

With context from subsystem 2 and the rest of the rulebook, I can reasonably conclude that subsystem 1 does not contain motors or electronics; it is only the mechanisms, such as wheels, that will aid in moving. Subsystem 2 is all of the motors and electronics for subsystem 1, including the brain. In reference to subsystem 1 (and therefore subsystem 2) rule also specifies, "the flat playing field". this implies that climbing mechanisms are not a part of subsystem 1 and subsystem 2 . this seems like an odd clarification for this year's competition, but this rule is simply carried over from previous years, and it makes sense in the context of previous competitions. This means that if we want to make a climbing mechanism to climb a stack of pins and cups, it is not limited to, or contribute to the 55W drive limit. This also means we cannot make a PTO from drive to climb, or use the same motors statically for driving and climbing due to rule R11 b, quoted below:

Appendix - R11

Motors are limited for Subsystem 2 (see <R1>). Robots may use any combination of V5 Smart Motors, 11W (276-4840) and/or 5.5W (276-4842), in Subsystem 2 within the following criteria:

  • a. The combined power of all motors in Subsystem 2 must not exceed 55W.
  • b. Motors used in Subsystem 2 cannot provide power to any mechanism that is not a part of Subsystem 1.
    • i. Motors in Subsystem 2 cannot be toggled, engaged, or configured such that they are capable of providing power to any part of the Robot that is not a part of Subsystem 1.
  • c. Teams may be required to demonstrate what each motor is capable of powering on their Robot during inspection in order to satisfy this requirement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
The rules that shape what we can build (see rule-analysis.md):

  • Start size: 18" x 18" x 18" (SG1)
  • Horizontal expansion: never bigger than 24" x 24" footprint at any point (SG2)
  • Vertical expansion: never taller than 50" (SG3); this applies the whole match, so during the 1:45 we can go tall freely up to 50"
  • SG12 (soft vertical cap) only applies in the ENDGAME midfield: the last 0:10, and only for robots in the midfield. It does not restrict tall stacking during normal play.
  • Possession: max 1 pin + 1 cup at once (SG6), the big constraint on hoarding
  • Preload: 1 pin (SG5)
  • Motors: 55W combined on subsystem 2; climbing mechanisms are outside that limit but can't share motors with the drive (R11b); see rule-analysis
  • Don't touch opposing alliance goals (SG9) or opposing load zones in driver control (SG13)
  • Match loads only enter through your own loaders, driver control only (SG11)

docs.title: Climbing bot
docs.text: Climb the stack to place from the top. Climbing isnt not allowed During normal play we can be tall (up to 50", SG3); But climbing lets us make really tall towers makeing the risk of loseing toggles lower (dont need to keep as many toggles) Main cost is placement speed from height vs. cycle time.

docs.title: Lifted by sister-team bot
docs.text: Partner lifts us to reach height or reposition without carrying our own lift mass. No rule against it. Cost is coordination (both robots committed), but the "free height / free reposition" same advantages as climbing

docs.title: Shooting / tossing bot
docs.text: = throwing one pin or cup on top of a stack. Under SG6 we can possess 1 at a time, and there's no rule against releasing/tossing a scoring object as long as it ends up placed (nested). So this is legal; the hard part is precision (landing it nested + keeping the scoring half visible), not very feasable, but also not impossable.

docs.title: Flying bot
docs.text: Not technically illegal: no rule says the robot must stay on the ground (S4 only penalizes being fully outside the field). The fun is the math: can a V5-legal robot generate enough lift/thrust within the 24"x24"x50" envelope? TODO: do the physics, thrust-to-weight with V5 motors + props made from legal vex parts, is it even close? Probably not, but it would be fun to do the math :3

docs.title: Jump bot
docs.text: Technically possible if you "get gud": a spring / stored-energy / pneumatic hop to clear traffic or reach the midfield. Pneumatics are limited (R25/R26) and it's risky, but not banned. Feasibility question: how much height can we get from legal stored energy?

docs.title: Scissor lift
docs.text: Legal, reaches stack height. Slow, and watch the 24" footprint as it extends (SG2). Classic but cycle-time-heavy.

docs.title: Fast bot
docs.text: Cycle time is the binding constraint (see the max score analysis); raw speed = points. Strong baseline that any of the above can be layered onto.

docs.title: Where the points actually are (from the max score analysis)
docs.text:
1. Yellow pins are 2x alliance-color pins, but only when owned; ownership comes from toggles (per quadrant) and midfield robot majority (endgame). Control ownership → the yellow value is yours instead of theirs. Massive swings.
  2. Cycle time beats stack height. SG6's 1-pin-1-cup cap means every score is a round trip. A fast, reliable placer that keeps the scoring half visible outscores a tall stacker.
  3. Endgame midfield = 8 pts/robot + the yellow-midfield ownership tiebreaker.

docs.title: Identify
docs.text:
Last season, our team management was not very well structured, this led to a "single-point-of-failure" where 90% of the designing and building was performed by one person. This is very clear when looking at this from last seasons notebook:

Overall Contribution History (2025-2026) Clover: 68.9% | 14684 words | 55 imgsLinus: 20.7% | 4861 words | 30 imgsParker: 8.4% | 2138 words | 0 imgsZach: 2.0% | 767 words | 4 imgs

The Problems we had last season:

  • Member Burnout: Over-reliance on one individual.
  • Knowledge Concentration: Because so much of the initial work was done by one person that one person can most of the knowledge leading to worse interview/design 'scores'
  • (Semi)-Neglected Tasks: Tasks like sponsor outreach and game analysis were not performed that well due to the fact that no one was specifically assigned those jobs
  • Interview Friction: Judges look for teams where "all students answer questions independently," which is impossible if only one person knows how the robot works.

docs.title: Brainstorm
docs.text:
Ideas to fix these problems:

Member burnout - Have at least 2 people that are assigned to every job - Start earlier in the season to spread out workload

Knowledge Concentration - Have at least 2 people that are assigned to every job - Document everything well - Work alongside people as much as possible not alone

Neglected Tasks - Make sure to assign people to every needed task - In team meetings discuss what was done for each task

Interview Friction - Solved with above solutions
